evidence_summary: A new-goods DiFiore's Music House advertisement dated Jan 18 1968 establishes Manny's Fuzz in commercial distribution outside New York City; a separate collector account places an owned example at the same Cleveland retailer in 1967-1968. Factory remains unresolved.

A used Orpheum Fuzz classified in the Sep 13 1968 St. Louis Post-Dispatch demonstrates circulation well beyond New York; the source treats prior new retail availability as likely, but not as a factory clue.

Clark-branded fuzz is documented in an Oct 5 1968 Syracuse used-gear ad; Clark's own manufacturing/distribution identity and firsthand employee evidence for wiring fuzz boxes support a genuine Clark production or assembly role, but do not prove Clark made every East Coast variant.

relationship_type: marketed identity / possible regional OEM state
evidence_summary: Fuzzboxes identifies Gracin's Fubar as a likely New York music-store branded member of the East Coast Fuzz family, but its manufacturing source remains unresolved.
AAT Fuzzier is a recognized East Coast Fuzz variant and shares the later three-knob enclosure family with Gracin's and Andre, but the evidence does not establish who physically built it.

Gene Andre is documented as an independent New Jersey repair/custom-shop operator from 1969; surviving Andre effects share construction details with East Coast Fuzz variants, but a common upstream OEM remains a plausible alternative to Andre as original builder.
Effects Database groups MGI with Clark, Orpheum, Manny's, Andre, AAT, Gracin's, and related East Coast Fuzz variants; no direct factory attribution is established in the cited sources.
Mica-Tone Fuzz appears in the documented East Coast family and also shares the regional reverb-product trail, but current evidence does not justify assigning a physical builder.

Fuzzboxes and Tone Machines identify the E.U. Wurlitzer unit as a distinct East Coast variant; a 1967 component-date clue is noted elsewhere, but marketplace claims tying it to Apollo or Orpheum are excluded as factory evidence.

Gilsonite Music Industries was an established New Jersey music business, but the cited corporate/legal record does not establish that Gilsonite physically built its East Coast Fuzz variant. Keep business existence separate from pedal manufacture.
Halifax is listed as an East Coast Fuzz variant and appears in the associated reverb-product evidence; current sources do not establish a physical builder.

Current specialist sources support a broader New York/New Jersey East Coast Fuzz family derived from early Mosrite Fuzzrite design, with multiple marketed identities and at least three enclosure states; common physical-builder identity remains unresolved.
